root.note: Latin aqua is secure. Its earlier Indo-European origin is not settled.

history: Acqua is Latin aqua, nearly unchanged, apart from the spelling. Italian writes cq where Latin had q: acqua, acquistare, nacque, tacque. The double sound is real, so you pronounce a long k before the w: ak-kwa. The Romance languages share the word, in Spanish agua, in Portuguese água and in French eau, which came from an older aigue. English aquarium, aquatic and aqueduct are learned borrowings from Latin, and Italian acquedotto is the same word in a native form. In Italy the choice is acqua del rubinetto, tap water, or acqua in bottiglia. At a restaurant you will be asked naturale o frizzante?, still or sparkling, and the water costs extra.
historyEinfach: Acqua is Latin aqua with Italian spelling. Italian writes cq in acqua, with a long k sound. French eau and Spanish agua are relatives, and so are English aquarium and aquatic. In a restaurant: naturale or frizzante?

elsewhere.text: French changed the word more than any other Romance language. Today it is a single vowel sound, written with three letters.
